text:
The mother dragon bent over the hatchling. With a low rumble, she curved her body around the little creature and sheltered it beneath one broad wing. The hatchling pressed close to her, safe and dry.

Ekin and Duru watched the two dragons settle together.

Relief warmed Ekin for a moment. Then she remembered the flash of brass vanishing into the wild sea. Her hand moved toward the place where her grandfather’s compass should have been.

Duru noticed. “We can’t go after it in this storm.”

Ekin’s first answer rose sharp in her throat, but she stopped it. Duru had guided her through the lighthouse and helped save the hatchling. She had earned the right to be heard.

“The compass is gone,” Ekin said. The words hurt, but she did not turn toward the sea. “I hate that it’s gone. But I’m not risking us to chase it anymore.”

Duru held her gaze, saw that she meant it, and nodded.

Rain still drove past the open upper-room door. Thunder rolled over the headland.

“I know the way back,” Duru said.

“This time,” Ekin replied, “I’ll follow.”

Duru stepped through the open upper-room door and reached the coastal path.

Ekin stepped through the same door and reached the coastal path beside her.

They returned together along the established coastal route. The storm continued throughout their journey, lashing rain across their faces and shaking the coast with thunder. Both girls saw the dark clouds crowding the sky and kept going.

Duru followed the established coastal path all the way into the harbor.

A step behind her, Ekin followed the established coastal path all the way into the harbor.

At last Ekin drew level with Duru. She did not call her a friend, not yet. But when Duru chose the next safe stretch ahead, Ekin trusted her and stayed beside her.
